ground_truth.unit: percentage points of the monthly hiring probability per percentage point of state unemployment
ground_truth.location: Table 1, Panel B, column (1), PE <= 10 x U. Rate
ground_truth.context: Table 1 ("Hiring Over the Business Cycle: With and Without Controls"), Panel B, column (1), row PE <= 10 x U. Rate.  Linear probability model (Equation 1 of the paper) of an indicator equal to 100 if the individual is hired in month t — begins a job at a new firm, either from non-employment in month t-1 or, if employed in t-1, reporting a change of employer since last month; new jobs classified as self-employment are not hires — on an indicator for potential experience (age minus years of education minus six) of at most ten years, and the state monthly unemployment rate interacted with each of the two potential-experience groups (at most ten years; more than ten years), with no main effect of the unemployment rate.  Column (1) has no fixed effects.  Sample: the matched monthly CPS panel, January 1994 to September 2016 (pairs of consecutive months matched on administrative IDs and confirmed on sex, race and age, following Madrian and Lefgren; May-August 1995 and month pairs spanning the eight-month sampling break excluded), civilians over 16 with non-missing age and education, all labour-force statuses in t-1.  Weighted by the average of the two months' CPS sampling weights; standard errors clustered by state (51 including DC).  The coefficient is the young workers' hiring response to one percentage point of state unemployment.

cell.label: claude-code
deviations_manifest: yh_data.csv (about 2 GB) read with data.table::fread(select=) of only the 19 columns the claimed specifications use, to fit the sandbox's 300 s / 4 GB limits.

Hiring regressions (Table 1 Panels A/B, Table 2) estimated by weighted least squares on cells of state x month x demo2 x young x prior labour-force status, with the cell weight being the sum of the CPS weights and the outcome being the weighted mean of hired100. Every regressor and fixed effect is constant within a cell, so the point estimates equal those of the person-level aweighted regression; the clustered-SE small-sample factor uses the number of cells instead of persons. The wage regression (Table 10) is run at person level.
Stata's m:1 crosswalk merges are done as lookups on keys deduplicated by (code, code-year).
deviations_stdout: yh_data.csv read with data.table::fread(select=) of only the 19 columns used (memory/time limits of the sandbox)

hiring regressions (Tables 1-2) estimated by WLS on state x month x demo2 x young x prior-status cells with summed CPS weights; identical point estimates to the person-level aweighted regression, clustered SE small-sample factor uses cell count
cell.notes: Followed YH_data_init.do and YH_regs.do: hired2 x 100 outcome, young = potential experience <= 10, youngurate/oldurate interactions, demo2 = group(minority, female, hisp, educ), state + month-year + demo2 fixed effects, CPS weight (v2pwsswgt+pwsswgt)/2, state-clustered SEs, fixef.rm='none'. Sample: exp and state unemployment rate non-missing (N = 16,948,516, matching the paper). Table 10 Panel B col 1: log real weekly wage of new hires with v2prwernal==0, with occupation (2002 recode) and industry (2002 recode) fixed effects (N = 112,858). attempt-1 was an exploratory read/timing run with no RESULT lines. attempt-2 was the first scored run; check_attempt reported every claim within tolerance. The only change after it was printing n_obs_full_sample as an exact integer (%.6g had rounded it to 1.69485e+07). The final run reproduces all 13 claims.
